title: Known at Ignalina in 1983: the Scram Defect Nobody Corrected, and the Announcement That Waited
participants: Chief Design Engineer for RBMK reactors
USSR State Committee for the Supervision of Safety in Industry and Nuclear Power (SCSSINP)

extractionLoop.stage1_upfrontSkim: The saving here was made in advance and in kind, not in cash: a design change that was promised and never made. The positive scram effect — reactivity added, rather than removed, in the first moments of inserting the control and safety rods — was identified at the Ignalina RBMK plant in Lithuania in 1983. The Chief Design Engineer for RBMK reactors circulated the finding to the other RBMK stations and said design changes would be made to correct it. INSAG’s 1992 report records what followed: "he made no such changes, and the procedural measures he recommended for inclusion in plant operating instructions were not adopted."
extractionLoop.stage2_structuralCompromise: A second promise went the same way. After Ignalina the chief engineering organization told every RBMK plant that it intended to impose restrictions on withdrawing the control and safety rods completely from the core; "Such restrictions were never imposed and apparently the matter was forgotten." A 1975 event at the Leningrad plant had already shown that local reactivity feedback could damage a reactor. INSAG’s verdict on the pair of precursors: "It is a matter of great concern that this important information was not adequately reviewed and, where it was disseminated to designers, operators and regulators, its significance was not fully understood and it was essentially ignored."
extractionLoop.stage3_informationFog: The fog operated in two directions at once, and both are documented. Outward, toward the public: "the Soviet government delayed the public announcement that the accident had occurred. Information provision was selective and restrictive, particularly in the immediate aftermath of the accident", and reliable information "was initially unavailable to the affected people". The cost was measurable — countermeasures against radioiodine in milk were "only partially effective ... because of the lack of timely information about the accident and necessary responses, particularly for private farmers". Inward, toward the people sent to find out what had happened: the design flaw was not disclosed at the IAEA’s own post-accident review in 1986, and INSAG said so in 1992: "Certainly the account in INSAG-1 would have been different had the features of the control and safety rods been revealed at the Post-Accident Review Meeting in 1986."
extractionLoop.stage4_monopolyWindfall: There is no commercial windfall in this record, and inventing one would be the easy, false move. What the documents show instead is a state that protected an industrial programme and its designers by controlling what the operators, the regulators, the public and finally the international review body were each allowed to know, and which was still protecting them a year after the reactor had destroyed itself.
extractionLoop.stage5_merseyWhitewash: The containment was the 1986 review itself, and its undoing is the reason the 1992 report exists. INSAG-7 is an official body publishing a correction to its own earlier findings once the withheld fact had surfaced — first acknowledged by Soviet experts at a Vienna conference in 1987, five years before the correction was printed. Its judgment is unusually direct for the genre: "It is reprehensible that such a deficiency had been known of for so long without its having been eliminated."

closedLoopRatchet.inheritedFramework: A nuclear programme whose designer, operator and regulator answered to the same state, and an information regime in which an industrial defect was a matter for the ministry rather than for the plants running the reactor.
closedLoopRatchet.newFrameworkCreated: The international convention, after 1986, that an accident at a nuclear plant is a matter of mandatory notification and assistance rather than of national discretion — and, in INSAG-7 itself, the precedent of a safety review body publicly reversing its own report when it learns it was not told everything.
closedLoopRatchet.closedLoopRecirculation: Each layer of silence protected the one above it. The design organisation was spared the cost of a retrofit by not enforcing its own instruction; the operators were spared knowledge they would have had to act on; the public was spared an announcement; and the review that should have caught all of it was spared the one fact that would have changed its account.

decoyVsLedger.viralDecoy: That the Party elite knew what had happened at once and quietly evacuated their own families while ordinary Ukrainians were marched out under the fallout for the May Day parades.
decoyVsLedger.whyDecoyFails: No document read for this dossier records any of it. The IAEA’s INSAG-7 is a report on reactor design, operation and regulation and says nothing about the evacuation of anyone. The Chernobyl Forum’s own report, which does cover the evacuation in detail, records no separate or earlier removal of officials, Party members or their families, and does not mention the May Day observances of 1 May 1986 at all. What it does record cuts across the simple version in both directions: the delay was real and the information regime was "selective and restrictive", and at the same time the authorities distributed stable iodine in Pripyat in the first hours — which "reduced the thyroid dose of the residents of Pripyat by a factor of 6 on average" — and evacuated about 50,000 people from the city within 40 hours. A dossier that asserted the nomenklatura evacuation would be asserting something it had not read.
decoyVsLedger.documentedLedger: The foreknowledge in this file is engineering foreknowledge, and it is documented to the year. The positive scram effect was identified at Ignalina in 1983; the Chief Design Engineer circulated it and promised design changes that were never made; the procedural measures he recommended were not adopted; the restrictions on full rod withdrawal were announced and never imposed. A 1975 Leningrad event had pointed the same way. The defect was not disclosed to the IAEA’s post-accident review in 1986 and was first acknowledged by Soviet experts in Vienna in 1987; INSAG published the correction in 1992 and called the delay reprehensible. On the public side: the announcement was delayed, information was selective and restrictive, the shortfall measurably reduced the effectiveness of countermeasures against radioiodine in milk, and the early secrecy is cited by the Forum as the reason official information on Chernobyl is still distrusted. Pripyat, about 50,000 people, was evacuated within 40 hours; more than 100,000 within a few weeks; 116,000 from the Exclusion Zone across the spring and summer of 1986; another 220,000 relocated in later years.

citations.title: International Atomic Energy Agency, The Chernobyl Accident: Updating of INSAG-1 — A Report by the International Nuclear Safety Advisory Group, Safety Series No. 75-INSAG-7 (Vienna, 1992)
citations.quoteOrFact: Downloaded from the IAEA's own publications server and read as extracted text. INSAG-7 exists because INSAG-1, the 1986 post-accident review, was written without a fact the Soviet side held. On the positive scram effect — the insertion of reactivity caused by the design of the control and safety rods — the report records: "The existence of the positive scram effect was first acknowledged by Soviet experts at the Conference on Nuclear Power Performance and Safety in Vienna in 1987. The SCSSINP Commission report states that this phenomenon had been known of at the time of the accident and that it had first been identified at the Ignalina RBMK plant in the Lithuanian Republic in 1983 ... Although the Chief Design Engineer for RBMK reactors promulgated this information to other RBMK plants, and stated that design changes would be made to correct the problem, he made no such changes, and the procedural measures he recommended for inclusion in plant operating instructions were not adopted. Apparently, there was a widespread view that the conditions under which the positive scram effect would be important would never occur. However, they did appear in almost every detail in the course of the actions leading to the accident." It further records that after the Ignalina discovery the chief engineering organization "informed other organizations and all nuclear power plants with RBMK reactors that it intended to impose restrictions on the complete withdrawal of control and safety rods from the core. Such restrictions were never imposed and apparently the matter was forgotten." INSAG's own verdict on this: "it does not really matter whether a positive scram was the final step that caused the reactor's destruction. It only matters that such a deficiency existed and that it could have been the cause of the accident. It is reprehensible that such a deficiency had been known of for so long without its having been eliminated." On what the 1986 international review was told, it says plainly: "Certainly the account in INSAG-1 would have been different had the features of the control and safety rods been revealed at the Post-Accident Review Meeting in 1986." Its summary conclusion (4) records that the rod effect "was a result of faulty design of the rods, the nature of which had been discovered at the Ignalina nuclear power plant in 1983. However, no correction was made following this discovery at Ignalina, no compensatory measures were taken and any dissemination of information to operating organizations was not followed up." Section 5.4 adds the 1975 Leningrad event as a second ignored precursor and states: "It is a matter of great concern that this important information was not adequately reviewed and, where it was disseminated to designers, operators and regulators, its significance was not fully understood and it was essentially ignored." The report is about reactor design, operation and regulation. It says nothing about the evacuation of anyone, nothing about the May Day parades, and nothing about the movements of officials or their families.

citations.title: The Chernobyl Forum 2003–2005 (IAEA, WHO, UNDP, FAO, UNEP, UN-OCHA, UNSCEAR, World Bank, Belarus, the Russian Federation and Ukraine), Chernobyl's Legacy: Health, Environmental and Socio-Economic Impacts, second revised version
citations.quoteOrFact: Downloaded from the IAEA's own site and read as extracted text (parts of the PDF carry a font-encoding fault that garbles some passages; nothing garbled is quoted here). On what was and was not told: "Unfortunately, reliable information about the accident and the resulting dispersion of radioactive material was initially unavailable to the affected people in what was then the Soviet Union and remained inadequate for years following the accident." Among the report's findings on the social consequences: "Third, the Soviet government delayed the public announcement that the accident had occurred. Information provision was selective and restrictive, particularly in the immediate aftermath of the accident." And on its long shadow: "Overcoming mistrust of information provided on Chernobyl remains a major challenge, owing to the early secrecy with which Soviet authorities treated the accident". The same silence had a measurable radiological cost: agricultural countermeasures "were only partially effective in reducing radioiodine intake via milk because of the lack of timely information about the accident and necessary responses, particularly for private farmers." On the evacuation itself the report is specific, and records action as well as delay: "Pripyat was the largest city nearest to the Chernobyl nuclear plant and approximately 50 000 residents were evacuated within 40 hours after the accident", while the intake of stable iodine tablets in the first hours after the accident "reduced the thyroid dose of the residents of Pripyat by a factor of 6 on average" (the number of hours stated there falls inside a font-garbled run in this PDF and was not readable, so it is not given); "More than 100 000 people were evacuated within few weeks after the accident from the most contaminated areas"; 116 000 people were evacuated in the spring and summer of 1986 from the Exclusion Zone and "Another 220 000 people were relocated in subsequent years." WHAT IS NOT IN IT: no separate or earlier evacuation of officials, Party members or their families is recorded anywhere in this report, and the May Day observances of 1 May 1986 are not mentioned at all.
